name: Classical republicanism
summary: Classical republicanism holds that a free political community is a res publica, a public thing governed by its citizens under law for the common good. It prizes civic virtue and active participation, a mixed constitution that balances monarchic, aristocratic and popular elements, a citizen militia in place of mercenaries or standing armies, and a vigilance against corruption by faction, wealth and personal power. Liberty means independence from arbitrary power, not mere non-interference.
scope: The tradition from Aristotle, Polybius and Cicero through Machiavelli's Discourses, Harrington and the English commonwealthmen to the American Founders, as presented in Wikipedia's article and the Stanford Encyclopedia entry. It follows the common core of the civic-humanist and neo-Roman readings and excludes modern republican parties, anti-monarchist movements and Kantian republicanism. Most social and economic statements were never addressed and are low-confidence inferences or 0.

keyFigures.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
keyFigures.role: Author of the Discourses on Livy, the central Renaissance statement of republican thought.

keyFigures.name: Cicero
keyFigures.role: Roman author of De re publica, which defines the res publica as the property of a people.

keyFigures.name: James Harrington
keyFigures.role: English republican whose ideal was an empire of laws and not of men.

sources.usedFor: Cicero's dialogue on the commonwealth, justice and virtue; thin on specifics.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The tradition never discussed health care; SEP notes only that modern republicans extend non-domination to basic-needs deprivation, which classical writers did not, so adherents are split.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Wage law is absent from classical texts; Machiavelli wanted citizens kept modest but no wage regulation is attested, so the answer is split.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Commerce and the monied interest are treated as sources of corruption in Pocock's account, and Machiavelli prefers a frugal citizenry, so adherents are wary of market primacy.

public-ownership.rationale: Machiavelli wants a rich public treasury and poor citizens (I.37), but nothing addresses nationalising industry; inferred and split.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Agrarian-law debates (I.37) aimed to curb the ambition of the great and keep wealth from overmatching the commons, which suggests mild support for burdening the wealthy.

unions-good.rationale: Trade bodies as such are not part of the classical tradition; guilds in Renaissance republics were mixed in role, so no clear stand.

property-fundamental.rationale: Pocock's civic ideal bases personality on property yet completes it in citizenship, and property is subordinate to the public good, so it is neither absolute nor dismissed.

regulate-corporations.rationale: The tradition fears a monied interest corrupting government, so tighter control of concentrated commercial power fits, though corporations are anachronistic.

cut-welfare.rationale: Classical republics distributed land and grain to keep the commons content (agrarian laws, I.37), and corruption was blamed on dependence on the great rather than on relief.

worker-ownership.rationale: Not discussed; widespread small property suits the ideal but collective firm ownership is not a republican theme.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Non-domination makes any unchecked government power over citizens suspect, so security surveillance without strong checks would be resisted.

legalize-drugs.rationale: The tradition addressed vice mainly through civic education and morals; drug policy was never taken up, so adherents split between liberty and virtue concerns.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Republicans valued free speech for public contest but also censured corrupting speech; no settled position is documented.

strong-leader.rationale: Machiavelli I.34 allows a temporary legal dictator but warns that unrestricted authority for a long term is dangerous and quickly corrupts a people (I.35); the tradition centres on rule of law against personal rule.

state-harmful.rationale: The tradition holds liberty is secured by a well-ordered republic under law, with the state as the means of non-domination, not as an evil.

limit-guns.rationale: The tradition favoured an armed citizenry as against standing armies (Pocock), so strict limits on arms sit badly with it, though modern regulation was not addressed.

empower-police-military.rationale: Standing armies are listed among the means of corruption and opposed to the militia ideal, so more power for professional forces is disfavoured.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Civic virtue and moral censorship were valued, which leans against it, but the issue was not directly discussed.

decide-locally.rationale: SEP notes writers sought cooperative and federal arrangements; the city-state model implies local self-government, though Rome itself centralised.

rehabilitation.rationale: Machiavelli stresses firm punishment of those threatening the republic (III.3) while accusations channel grievances; reform of offenders is not attested.

traditional-family.rationale: Patriarchal household was assumed in classical sources, but the tradition rests on civic not familial foundations; adherents vary.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Not addressed; civic republicans today support it, classical authors did not discuss it, so split.

abortion-legal.rationale: No documented position; inferred split between civic-moral and liberty considerations.

more-religion-public.rationale: Machiavelli (I.11-12) praises Numa's use of religion to bind citizens to oaths and law, and the German free states' devout spirit (I.55), so religion as civic glue is valued.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Anachronistic; SEP says modern republicans treat exclusion as removable prejudice, but classical adherents did not address it.

gender-social-construct.rationale: The tradition did not take up the question; SEP records patriarchal assumptions only.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Patriotism and civic attachment to the republic's laws and customs were central values (Bartholomew of Lucca, Roman republican values), so preserving its way of life matters.

gradual-change.rationale: Founders such as Machiavelli's lawgiver (I.9) favour decisive founding acts, yet praise institutions that grew through conflict (I.4) and stress renewal toward first principles, so split.

reduce-immigration.rationale: SEP notes confinement of freedom to native-born men; however immigration levels were not an issue Roman or Florentine writers debated as policy.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The tradition rests on self-governing polities; SEP records federal arrangements as a response to empire, but supranational power over a republic conflicts with self-rule.

free-trade.rationale: Commerce and monied interests were seen as corrupting, and Machiavelli favours self-reliance, so free trade as universal benefit is doubtful.

nation-first.rationale: Patriotism and the republic's independence take priority in the tradition, though classical republicans also sought alliances.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Sidney's maxim that swords exist so none are slaves, not to enslave others, and worry about imperial conquest, point against crusading abroad.

open-borders.rationale: A republic built on a bounded citizen body with civic ties and a defined people (Cicero) is hard to reconcile with open borders.

limit-growth.rationale: Not attested; Machiavelli's frugality ideal and fear of corruption by wealth sit against his call for expansion (I.6).

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Anachronistic; no basis in the tradition beyond general common-good concern.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: The tradition stresses virtue and institutions over material progress as the cure for political ills.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Energy policy is outside the tradition and no republican principle bears on it.

revolution-justified.rationale: Republican writers like Milton and Sidney justified removing tyrants, and the American Founders drew on them for resistance against domination.

experts-over-public.rationale: Machiavelli (I.58 title, I.47) holds the people judge well and are the best guardians of liberty (I.5), and citizen participation is central.

central-planning.rationale: Not discussed; widespread property and citizen self-rule do not fit central planning.

socialized-markets.rationale: Not addressed by classical republicans; widespread ownership is welcome, but the formula is modern.

land-value-tax.rationale: Land limits were debated through agrarian laws (I.37), but a single land tax was not proposed.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Agrarian laws capped holdings to restrain the great, which supports curbing concentrated wealth, but inheritance taxes were not discussed.

basic-income.rationale: Republics distributed land and kept citizens self-reliant and active; unconditional stipends would breed dependence, but this is inferred.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: No documented position; self-reliance leans for, anti-corruption of trade does not decide it.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Machiavelli wants a rich public treasury, but directing investment is not attested.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Pocock's account makes property the base of citizen personality and independence, and Machiavelli favours great equality of condition in a commonwealth (I.55).

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Nothing in the tradition suggests it; property is tied to citizen independence.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Anachronistic; the tradition feared the monied interest but did not discuss central banks.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Corporatist state bodies are not a feature; republicans would fear organised sectional interests as corruption.

one-party-rule.rationale: Machiavelli I.4 praises the conflict of nobles and plebs as the source of free laws, and the tradition's mixed constitution rejects any single faction holding the state.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Plato, Aristotle, Polybius and Cicero include a monarchic element in the mixed constitution, and More and Smith saw law-bound monarchy as compatible, yet Dutch and Bruni views call monarchy corrupt; adherents split.

democracy-best.rationale: The tradition prefers a mixed constitution over pure democracy, though it gives the people a key role; so democracy alone is not endorsed as best.

direct-votes.rationale: Classical republics did use popular assemblies, but the tradition's mixed constitution and checks on mass passions disfavour government by direct vote on major laws.

workers-councils.rationale: Councils as political base were never proposed; mixed constitution with senate and assemblies is the model.

right-to-secede.rationale: The tradition prizes the republic's integrity and union, and does not discuss a right to leave.

natural-rulers.rationale: Plato paired civic virtue with the personal virtue of rulers and the mixed constitution gives the few a role; Cicero and Aristotle see some as better fit to rule.

political-violence-never.rationale: Machiavelli defends Romulus's killing of Remus for the common good (I.9) and republicans justified tyrannicide, so violence is sometimes justified.

war-builds-character.rationale: Machiavelli I.6 says a republic needs a great and warlike population, and Polybius links Rome's institutions to conquest; martial virtue is prized.

separate-church-state.rationale: Religion is valued as civic instrument (I.11), yet American republicans opposed established churches and Cromwell's was a Christian republic; adherents split.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Laws come from the lawgiver's reason and the people, with religion as support; Machiavelli treats religion as a tool of order, not a source of statute.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Defence by citizens and public courts is central; Machiavelli says mercenary troops are worthless (I.43).

military-superiority.rationale: Machiavelli stresses strength to hold and expand (I.6), though SEP notes worry about empire; mild support.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Republicans defined the people by shared law and interest (Cicero), not ethnicity, but confined citizenship to native-born men; split.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Machiavelli I.4 makes noble-plebeian conflict central to Rome's freedom, but does not call it the driving force of all history.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Machiavelli seeks a great equality of condition in a commonwealth (I.55) but no equal outcomes; honor remains a positional good (SEP).

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: The tradition never considered indigenous claims; Roman and Renaissance writers dealt with city-states, and no principle decides it.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Reparations are a modern idea; republicans condemned domination but did not address redress for past empire.

civilizational-union.rationale: The model is the self-governing polity, not unions by civilization.

self-interest-moral.rationale: SEP defines corruption as advancing personal or sectional interest at the expense of the public good and virtue as supporting that good.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Civic virtue requires willingness to put the public good first, though the instrumental reading values duties for securing liberty.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Environmental ethics did not figure in republican texts, and no civic principle settles it.

limit-population.rationale: Machiavelli wants a numerous warlike people (I.6), against limiting it.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Anachronistic; the tradition's critique of luxury and commerce gives some sympathy but no stated view.

accelerate-technology.rationale: The tradition prizes stability of institutions and fears disruption of balance.

human-enhancement.rationale: Bioenhancement is anachronistic; virtue-centred republicans might worry about it, while liberty favours choice, so split.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Rule by citizens and statesmen of virtue is the ideal; handing government to algorithms conflicts with it.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Anachronistic; non-domination favours privacy from arbitrary power, but no stated position.

restore-past-order.rationale: Machiavelli urges renewal toward first principles but also values new founding; adherents split.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Machiavelli judges by outcomes for the republic, yet adherents hold fixed constitutional principles.

direct-action.rationale: Machiavelli I.7-8 prefers lawful channels like accusation to extra-legal tumult.

means-match-ends.rationale: Machiavelli defends dubious means for the common good (I.9), others stress law, so split.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Contrary to the city-republic model of civic life.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Classical republics had distinct offices and orders; abolition not contemplated.

distribute-by-need.rationale: SEP says classical writers did not address basic needs; distribution by need is modern.

production-for-use.rationale: Production aims were not discussed; the tradition cared about the independence of citizens, not the purpose of output.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Not a classical republican idea; property was the base of independence.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Class dictatorship contradicts the mixed constitution; the Roman dictatorship (I.34) was temporary and legal, not class-based.

collective-farming.rationale: Small independent holders underpin the civic ideal.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: SEP notes empire as a risk to republics, but capitalism-war thesis is not theirs.

taxation-theft.rationale: Machiavelli wants a rich public treasury (I.37), so taxation for common purposes is legitimate.

harm-principle.rationale: Republics legislate on morals and virtue, so the state may do more than prevent harm, though perfectionism is contested (civic humanist vs republican readings).

individual-rights-only.rationale: Classical republicans saw liberty as a product of society and stressed citizen duties over pre-social rights.

conscription.rationale: Machiavelli argues for arming your own subjects (I.43) and a national army (I.21 title), and the militia ideal presumes citizen service.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Liberty is exercised through participation; Bruni and Pocock stress active citizenship over exit.

state-as-business.rationale: Citizens are co-rulers of the public thing, not customers.

positive-liberty.rationale: Berlin tilted republicanism toward positive liberty, but Pettit's non-domination reading differs; SEP says modern republicans add need as threat to freedom.

media-academia-power.rationale: Republicans feared corruption of government by sectional interests, but a claim about media and universities was never made.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Not discussed; republicans grounded status on virtue and law not biology.

organic-representation.rationale: Representation through assemblies and magistrates, not family and trade bodies.

total-state.rationale: Machiavelli I.34-35 warns unrestricted authority corrupts a people, and the tradition holds liberty needs limits on all power.

national-rebirth.rationale: Machiavelli urges returning to origins to renew a republic, but not radical rebirth from decadence by a national movement.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Machiavelli I.6 argues expansion needed, Sidney and others warn against, so classical adherents split.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Harrington's empire of laws not men, and non-domination, oppose rule resting on personal loyalty.

bound-labor.rationale: Slavery is the paradigm of domination for republicans, and bound labor to a lord is dependence.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: The tradition shares Cicero's belief in reason and justice.

universal-morality.rationale: Cicero's Book III examines justice in government and the surviving dialogue assumes law grounded in universal justice.

single-common-good.rationale: Civic virtue is willingness to support the public good, but Machiavelli I.4 values the clash of orders, so not purely one good.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: A modern national question never taken up by classical republicans.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Citizenship by return of a diaspora was not addressed; the tradition links citizenship to membership of a political community.

revive-national-language.rationale: Language policy is not a theme, though Renaissance humanists revived Latin letters for civic purposes.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Self-rule applied to the state, not firms; neither endorsed nor opposed in the sources.

school-vouchers.rationale: SEP stresses civic education to sustain commitment; vouchers fit poorly with common schooling.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Machiavelli wants a rich treasury but stimulus not discussed.

economic-freedom.rationale: SEP's republican liberty is independence from arbitrary power, with property supporting it, but commerce is also feared.

rule-by-example.rationale: Plato paired civic virtue with ruler virtue, and Cicero's Book V concerns ideal citizen; but laws are the main instrument.

national-self-determination.rationale: Self-governing polity free from outside domination is the core idea, as Priestley on colonies.

force-without-un.rationale: No international body existed; republicans' only guide is that arms should defend liberty, not enslave others, which does not settle UN approval.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Cicero grounds law in reason, while Machiavelli values religion for civic use; adherents split.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Benefits would flow to citizens as members of the republic, inferred from native-born citizenship.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Active citizenship and self-reliance are prized over dependence.

class-collaboration.rationale: Machiavelli I.4 values the conflict of orders yet seeks concord under law.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Renaissance humanism revived classical heritage as the source of republican values.

dominated-front.rationale: Resisting domination by a power fits the tradition's logic, but a bloc against the West is a modern alignment not addressed.

workers-nation.rationale: Class or national organisation of workers is a modern debate with no counterpart in the tradition.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: SEP notes patriarchal confinement of public life to men, a feature of the classical writers, but later writers dropped it.

ban-interest.rationale: Not a stated aim; commerce was feared but usury bans are not documented.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Republican liberty is defined by equal citizens under law; racial classification is not part of the ideal, though ancient exclusions existed.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Machiavelli holds laws favourable to liberty arose from class conflict (I.4), so the state can serve the common good.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Energy production is outside the tradition and no principle decides it.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Civic belonging requires adopting the republic's laws and customs, inferred.

elite-replacement.rationale: Conspiracy theories of this kind are not part of republican thought; the tradition locates danger in corruption of institutions, not hidden plots over population.

proportional-representation.rationale: Not addressed; mixed constitution is about orders not parties.

national-mission.rationale: Machiavelli's expansion (I.6) and "rapacious republicanism" (s1) suggest mission, but SEP records Sidney's contrary view.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: SEP notes patriarchy in classical writers but they did not analyse it.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Corruption of officials and elites is the tradition's main worry, with remedies such as screening and sanctions.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Not addressed; Plato aside, civic tradition does not discuss it.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Machiavelli I.7-8 praises accusation of officials as a protection of liberty.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Machiavelli wants an active republic with education, religion and armed citizens, going far beyond minimal state.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Republican citizenship rests on law and shared advantage (Cicero), not descent, so discouraging unions has no basis, though the tradition is silent.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Equal rights for citizens under law is central, but political honor is a positional good and exclusions of non-citizens existed.

socialism-one-country.rationale: A Marxist debate with no republican counterpart.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Anachronistic framing; the tradition criticised colonial domination but did not classify settler states.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Equal citizens under one rule of law fits, but religious law not discussed.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Religion valued as civic glue, no stated policy on conversion.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: A religious-cultural prohibition with no basis in republican texts, though Machiavelli values religion as civic glue, so mildly opposed.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Civic education valued, religion as civic tool, split.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist doctrine; republicans fear standing power but also value defence, so no clear answer.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Cicero defines res publica as property of a people held together by agreement on law and shared advantage, though the tradition grounds legitimacy in non-domination more than consent.

trade-surplus.rationale: Machiavelli wants a rich treasury, but trade balance not discussed.

population-transfer.rationale: Not documented, and republican law protects members of the people.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Machiavelli accepts force for the common good (I.9, I.6), so the absolute rule is rejected.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Machiavelli credits conflict between orders for Rome's liberty and warlike expansion, but does not claim universal progress.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Machiavelli III.3 favours suppressing those who would restore tyranny, inferred.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: SEP states republican liberty is structural independence from arbitrary power and a slave whose master rarely interferes is still unfree.

separated-powers.rationale: Plato, Aristotle, Polybius and Cicero held the ideal republic mixes orders, and Machiavelli I.2 says each serves as a check on the others.

vanguard-party.rationale: The people as guardian of liberty (I.5) and mixed constitution reject vanguard rule.

priority-to-poor.rationale: SEP says classical writers did not address basic needs, though Machiavelli favours protecting the commons.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Housing policy is modern; widespread property supports it mildly but public housing is not discussed.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Industrial action is outside the tradition and neither order nor liberty principles decide.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Machiavelli ties poverty to institutions like agrarian law and inequality, not population.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Cicero stresses agreement on law and shared advantage, not ethnic uniformity.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Athenian practice used lot, Roman and Machiavellian practice used election (I.58, I.60); adherents split.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Machiavelli I.34 backs a temporary dictator but warns against unrestricted authority, so partial.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Machiavelli wanted the commons content but never discussed fixing prices, so no principle settles it.

party-controls-media.rationale: Government control of information conflicts with citizen accusation and open contest of orders (I.4, I.7).

party-commands-army.rationale: Machiavelli wants a citizen army (I.21, I.43) loyal to the republic, with civil control by the mixed constitution.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Native-born citizens and civic ties valued, inferred.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Republics expected officeholders to be citizens of means and often unpaid; low pay for representatives is not addressed.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Factions and parties were seen as corruption, but binding discipline is not discussed.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Federal arrangements were sought by some, but pooling sovereignty with larger union threatens self-rule.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Pocock's tradition opposes standing armies under executive and patronage; checks over the executive.

clerical-rule.rationale: Authority rests in citizens and magistrates; religion serves them.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Patriotism and defence of the republic are core virtues, so working for its defeat is disfavoured.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Civic virtue is a core concern and Plato paired civic virtue with the good, inferred.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Machiavelli I.34 warns authority conferred for a long term is dangerous, and the tradition fears personal power.

recall-officials.rationale: Machiavelli I.7 praises citizens' right to accuse magistrates, inferred.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Machiavelli stresses self-reliant arms (I.43), but Roman republic used allies, so adherents split.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Widespread property is favoured but compulsory ownership and a ban on renting was never proposed; inferred mild no.

people-in-arms.rationale: Machiavelli I.43 urges arming the natives of your country and calls mercenaries worthless; Pocock lists standing armies against the militia ideal.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Landed independence valued, Renaissance republics were commercial cities; split.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: National unification is a modern concern; city-republic writers did not take sides on it.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Humanist education was prized as the training of citizens, so the tradition disagrees with the claim.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Roman writers held their republic was the best constitution.

death-penalty.rationale: Machiavelli III.3 and Roman practice punish severe threats to the republic firmly.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Not a classical subject; civic education is valued but its content on sex is unaddressed.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Humanist learning and reason are prized, though Machiavelli values religion civically; mildly opposed.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Civic virtue and moral censorship consistent, inferred.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: SEP notes confinement to native-born, but not a doctrine.

minority-language-support.rationale: Languages were not a political issue for classical republics, and no principle decides it.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Equal rule of law favours uniform rules, but toleration of conscience is not a classical theme; split.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Civic conformity to public virtue valued.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: International debt relief is modern and not addressed.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Republicans tie freedom to property and equality of condition, but the claim concerns post-colonial settings never discussed.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Machiavelli I.9 says new institutions come from a single lawgiver, though maintained by many.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Liberty as non-domination is the central value and growth is not a stated end, so trading freedom for growth is disfavoured.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: SEP says classical writers did not address basic needs of distant strangers.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Anachronistic; self-reliance in arms (I.43) suggests mild yes.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Machiavelli I.58 prefers popular election of magistrates, but heads of state aren't discussed.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Central banks are modern; the tradition feared the monied interest but also arbitrary government.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Claims to land were not framed this way in the tradition; no principle decides it.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Pocock: property is perfected through citizenship, and Machiavelli I.37 would restrain holdings that threaten the republic.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: A Marxist debate outside republican concerns.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental risk regulation is anachronistic, though common-good duties could support it.

collective-defense.rationale: Machiavelli prefers own arms (I.43) over reliance on allies, but the Roman republic built alliances, so split.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Non-domination implies a people cannot be rightly held by a power it did not choose, as Priestley said of colonies subject to Parliament; inferred.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Established churches counted as corrupting (Pocock) and religion is subordinate to the republic, inferred.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Mixed constitutions had consuls or a monarchic element, but whether it is nonpartisan was not discussed.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: The tradition prizes the integrity of the republic; inferred.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Federal arrangements attracted some republicans (SEP), but specific autonomy deals are modern.

sacred-ruler.rationale: The republic's authority rests on law and citizens, not on divine descent.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Income taxation is modern; republicans wanted wealth restrained, which leans against, but not settled.

character-from-environment.rationale: SEP stresses civic education and culture as means to sustain virtue.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: SEP records Harrington's ideal of an empire of laws and not of men; a ruler above the law is the paradigm of arbitrary power.

space-expansion.rationale: Anachronistic; Machiavelli favours expansion by arms on earth but nothing on space.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Plato, Aristotle, Polybius and Cicero held the ideal republic mixes monarchy, aristocracy and democracy, and Machiavelli I.2 says a mixed constitution is more durable because each checks the others.

leader-cult.rationale: Personal glorification conflicts with the rule of law and fears of unrestricted authority corrupting a people (I.35).

equal-parenting.rationale: Custody law is outside the tradition.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist thesis with no counterpart in republican thought.

land-redistribution.rationale: Agrarian laws drove conflict (I.37), Machiavelli saw their mischief yet equality as basis; adherents split.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Cicero defines a people by law and advantage, not ethnicity.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Religion valued as civic tool, but punishing exit is not in the sources.

women-must-cover.rationale: Dress law for women has no basis in the tradition, which regulated virtue through civic education; mildly opposed.

common-currency.rationale: Anachronistic; republicans favoured self-governing polities, but currency union was not discussed.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: The model is the self-governing city or commonwealth defined by law, not unions of peoples by ancestry.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Republican writers did not address minority emigration or homelands.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Machiavelli sees laws and institutions as shaping outcomes (I.4).

ban-cartels.rationale: Concentrations of economic power feed corruption, inferred.

no-bailouts.rationale: The tradition distrusted the monied interest, leaning against bailouts, but also valued public treasuries, so unresolved.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Rule of law and mixed constitution restrain majorities; Cicero warns excessive liberty leads to servitude (I.68).

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Classical writers confined office to men; parity not a topic.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Machiavelli stresses self-reliance in arms but did not propose autarky or colonial blocs.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Modern trade law; no principle decides.

moral-incentives.rationale: Civic virtue and public esteem are what motivate service in the tradition (SEP).

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Not part of tradition; republic relies on citizen institutions.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Republican writers rejected monarchy and hereditary rule, yet mixed constitutions give the aristocracy standing; split.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Renaissance republicans taught Roman history as the civic model, and patriotic education is valued.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Machiavelli I.6 accepts expansion, but others warn against dominating others (Sidney).

patriotic-education.rationale: SEP says civic education and public esteem are needed to sustain citizens' commitment.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: A modern American policy debate not addressed in the tradition.

public-money-creation.rationale: Monetary arrangements are modern; the tradition distrusted private finance but this was not tied to money creation.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: A modern economic debate outside the tradition.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Machiavelli accepts expansion (I.6) but this is about influence after empire, not addressed.

delink-world-market.rationale: A development-theory debate absent from the tradition.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist claim unrelated to republican thought.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Private power over others is domination, which republicans oppose.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Rule of law and limits on power fit, but written bills of rights came later; the tradition favoured mixed institutions as checks.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Colonial boundary questions did not arise for classical republicans.

elective-rulers.rationale: Machiavelli I.58 and I.60 discuss election of magistrates by the people as the republic's method, against hereditary succession.

minority-veto.rationale: Machiavelli I.4 values conflict resolved by laws made by the orders, with no individual veto.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: SEP names Milton, Sidney, Harrington as republican writers and the Americans resisting Parliament as in servitude; a ruler outside the law exercises domination.

parliament-supreme.rationale: English republicans favoured legislatures over kings, but the mixed constitution gives no single body supremacy.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Cicero's ideal statesman serves the commonwealth with virtue (Book V), and elites owe it service.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Civic participation is central and Bruni argued republics produce better men; withdrawal is a vice.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: A Frankfurt School thesis; republicans feared luxury and corruption but not mass media.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: A Gramscian thesis outside the tradition.

native-born-offices.rationale: SEP records that classical writers confined freedom and office to propertied, native-born men.

party-own-road.rationale: A communist-movement question outside the tradition.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Machiavelli advocates self-reliance in arms (I.43), inferred.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Territorial revanchism was not discussed as doctrine.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Anachronistic; the tradition rested equal citizens under law, but did not address settler societies.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Anachronistic; republicans oppose tyranny but this is a twentieth-century constitutional formula.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Anachronistic; republicans condemn tyranny generally but the comparison was not theirs.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: A historical claim about the US not addressed; SEP counts slavery as the paradigm of domination, yet the historical-causation claim is outside the tradition.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Civic memory is valued but contested monuments are not addressed.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: A modern welfare debate outside the tradition.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: A modern policy debate not addressed.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Republicans held their form best but also that constitutions suit peoples' condition (Machiavelli I.55 on equality); unresolved.

military-guardian-role.rationale: The tradition is wary of armed force acting outside civil institutions; Tacitus (s1) traces how granting powers led to Augustus.

paid-care-work.rationale: Household labour was not a political theme for classical writers.

filial-duty.rationale: Roman republican values included family piety.

office-by-exam.rationale: Offices come through election by citizens (I.58, I.60).

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Anachronistic; independence of the republic suggests wariness, but not addressed.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Accountability valued (I.7) but instruction-bound delegates conflicts with magistrates' independence.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Pension design is modern and the sources say nothing about it; no republican principle decides between state and private schemes.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Property as base of citizen personality conflicts with tenure only for use.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: English country writers resisted court patronage and standing armies, inferred.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Land is bound to the citizen body in SEP's account of propertied, native-born citizens; restricting foreigners is an inference.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Modern anti-discrimination doctrine is outside the tradition, and no republican principle decides intent versus outcome.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Luxury and commerce corrupting; the tradition praised frugality (Machiavelli I.37 poverty of citizens).

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Sidney's maxim that swords exist so none may be slaves suggests aiding the oppressed, but arming insurgents is not attested; weak lean against.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Sidney: swords given so none be slaves.

corporate-influence.rationale: Pocock's monied interest and patronage are corruption.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Corruption by outside influence was feared (Machiavelli I.55 on foreign manners) but NGO funding was not discussed.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Machiavelli I.6 wants numerous people, inferred.

residents-only-property.rationale: Local land rules were not discussed.

job-guarantee.rationale: SEP says concern for basic needs is a modern republican addition, not classical.

democratic-peace.rationale: Machiavelli I.6 thinks republics expand through war.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Civic virtue requires supporting the public good and obeying laws of republic.

non-intervention.rationale: Sidney opposes enslaving others, but the tradition included war for expansion (Machiavelli I.6), so no firm doctrine.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Conspiracy claims about minorities are not part of the tradition.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Legal marriage and property were part of the civic order; abolition not proposed.

local-production.rationale: Local production was not a theme.

informal-organisation.rationale: Machiavelli favours public institutions and lawful accusation.

national-law-over-international.rationale: A self-governing republic's own laws bind its citizens, though international law was not the issue then; inferred.

religious-nation.rationale: Cicero's people is defined by law, not religion.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Non-domination rejects subordination of a state to another.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Property distinctions of this kind are Marxist and not addressed.

defeat-communism.rationale: Communism as a rival world system is a twentieth-century question, and the tradition offers no stance on coexistence versus defeat.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Mixed provision of public services is a modern administrative question that the tradition never addressed.

religion-illusion.rationale: Machiavelli treats religion as civic force with real effect (I.11).

capitalism-progressive.rationale: A Marxist claim outside republican thought.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Not addressed; SEP notes patriarchy but no economic thesis.

treaties-binding.rationale: Fidelity to oaths praised (Machiavelli I.11) but not treaty with internal nations.

cooperative-communities.rationale: The model is a polity under law, not commune.

majority-settlement.rationale: Settlement policy for ethnic groups is outside the sources; Cicero defines a people by law and shared advantage, not by ethnic settlement.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Claims based on historical or religious ties to land are not discussed in the republican sources, so no answer follows from them.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Not part of the tradition; the tradition values reason and truthful civic discourse.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Machiavelli I.4 and I.7-8 treat opposition and open accusation as the lifeblood of liberty.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Religion as civic glue supports; but no stated penalty.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Priestley called colonies subject to Parliament's taxes servants, and Sidney said swords are not given to enslave others, so ruling colonies for the metropole is domination.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: A religious doctrine foreign to the tradition.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Resistance is tied to lawless rule, not irreligion.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Greek republics involved extensive participation but classical writers favoured mixed institutions.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Legal recognition of gender identity is an anachronistic question that classical republican writers never raised.

assisted-dying.rationale: Medical end-of-life choice was not a theme of the tradition and no civic principle settles it.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Anachronistic; the mixed-constitution tradition itself mixes orders, but no stand on left-right.

alienated-labor.rationale: A Marxist concept outside republican thought.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Not part of the tradition and rests on grounds it did not hold.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Cicero grounds the res publica in a people joined by law; authority from people.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Ferry's laws belong to later French republicanism.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Employment contract rules of this kind are modern; the tradition only supplies general hostility to arbitrary private power.

social-market-economy.rationale: A social market economy is a postwar German model that the tradition never discussed, so no answer is inferable.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Machiavelli I.43 and I.21 title want a national army and a citizen militia.

rich-first.rationale: A development-policy slogan outside the tradition.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Alignment among great-power blocs not addressed.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Republics choose magistrates by election (I.58); hereditary monarchy considered corrupt by Bruni and de la Courts.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Mutualist credit schemes are outside the tradition.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Anachronistic, though independence from outside domination suggests sympathy.

property-franchise.rationale: SEP says classical writers confined freedom to propertied men and property is the base of independence.

domination-women-nature.rationale: An ecofeminist thesis outside the tradition.

reification.rationale: A Marxist concept outside republican thought.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Republicans feared wealth corrupting politics but press ownership is anachronistic.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: SEP records Harrington's ideal of an empire of laws and not of men, and Blackstone that where there is no law there is no freedom.

racial-franchise.rationale: The tradition limited the franchise by property and native birth, not race; no support for racial rule.

online-participation.rationale: Internet deliberation is anachronistic; the tradition values citizen participation but gives no view on its medium.

open-government-data.rationale: Open accusation and citizen oversight, inferred.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Marriage across religions was not a political question in the sources, so the tradition gives no answer.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Athenian lot and assemblies belong to the tradition, but selection by lot is not preferred by Roman republicans.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: The sources treat religion as a civic instrument (Machiavelli I.11), but reinterpreting doctrine is not discussed.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Machiavelli I.55 says a commonwealth belongs where great equality exists, and I.37 stresses curbing the ambition of the great.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Open service by gay soldiers was never addressed; the citizen-militia ideal concerns who bears arms for the republic, not orientation, so this is an unsourced inference and adherents are split.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Machiavelli treats religion as a support for civic virtue and oaths in the republic, so a state teaching unbelief runs against the tradition.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Inferred from the rule of law: republican liberty needs law enforced by magistrates and a citizen militia, so abolishing coercive enforcement has no place in it.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Inferred from the mixed constitution, which gives each order (one, few, many) a guaranteed share of power; the tradition balanced classes, not ethnic or religious communities.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The sources are silent on relief of the poor; the tradition prized frugal, independent citizens but also public grain and civic provision, so adherents are split.

term-limits.rationale: Inferred from the short, rotating magistracies and fear of lasting personal power in Rome and in Harrington's rotation; no source states a term-limit rule directly.

vote-delegation.rationale: Inferred from the ideal of citizens deliberating and voting in person in assemblies; revocable proxy voting is a modern idea the tradition never considered.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Extinction risk is anachronistic to the tradition; its concern with the republic's survival and corruption gives no clear answer.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Inferred from the tradition's exclusion of women from citizenship and public office (SEP on exclusions); religious office was never discussed separately.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Inferred from the tradition's household of the male citizen and its exclusion of women from public life; marital authority itself was not addressed.

missingStatements.text: Standing professional armies are a danger to a free state.
missingStatements.rationale: Pocock's account lists standing armies among the means of corruption, opposed to the militia ideal, and Machiavelli calls mercenaries worthless.

missingStatements.text: A free state needs a relative equality of condition among its citizens, and great concentrations of wealth endanger it.
missingStatements.rationale: Machiavelli I.55 says a commonwealth belongs where great equality exists, and I.37 stresses curbing the ambition of the great.

missingStatements.text: Luxury and the pursuit of wealth corrupt a people and undermine its liberty.
missingStatements.rationale: Corruption through monied interest and foreign manners is a standing theme in Pocock's account and Machiavelli I.55.
missingStatements.declined: Moralised claim about luxury and corruption, not a question other ideologies take sides on; the wealth-concentration statement captures the political core.

missingStatements.text: A people is wiser than a prince in choosing magistrates and guarding its liberty.
missingStatements.rationale: Machiavelli I.5 and the I.58 chapter title favour the commons as guardians of liberty over princes.
missingStatements.declined: Machiavelli-specific; democracy-best already covers trust in the people and this audit answers it neutrally, so the proposal does not map onto it.

notes: The civic-humanist reading treats participation as intrinsically good; the neo-Roman reading treats virtue as instrumental to non-domination. Classical sources confined citizenship to propertied native-born men, which modern republicans reject.
